page.title: Invoked services
page.description: Run a connection, a subprocess or a long computation for as long as a chart's state is active, with SCXML's invoke.

hero.headline: Keep a connection open while a state lasts
hero.lede: A chart's <invoke> starts a connection or a subprocess in your program when the chart enters a state, and stops it when the chart leaves. 200,000 actors with one each made a million round trips in 18 to 23 seconds.

section.heading: Choose invoke for work that outlives a request
section.p: An I/O processor answers one send at a time, while a connection or a subscription lives longer. SCXML's <invoke> starts it on entering a state and stops it on leaving.
While the state is active, the chart and what it invoked exchange events. When your program runs it, it is a service, the subject of this guide.
An invoked chart runs instead as a child actor of the host (A chart that starts another).

section.heading: Start a service when the state is entered
section.p: Register a handler per <invoke type> in the host's services: { [type]: handler }. At each start the handler gets an invocation and returns the service, any object.
The host keeps the service until the invocation ends, and calls two methods on it if it has them:

item.text: gets each <send target="#_<invokeid>"> of the invoker, and each event it forwards with autoforward="true";
runs when the invoker leaves the state, which cancels the invocation.

section.p: The service answers through the invocation. invocation.sendBack(event, data) sends the invoker an event whose _event.invokeid is the invoke's id.
invocation.done(data) ends the service and gives the invoker done.invoke.<invokeid> with data.
This counter starts from the invoke's start param, 10, answers each ping with pong, and ends on finish with its total:

example.code: started urn:example:counter counter://local for session 1 pong 11 from counter pong 12 from counter done, total 13

section.p: stop runs only for a cancel: the counter ended with done, so the output has no stopped.

section.heading: Send to a service from a later event
section.p: A service starts after the step that entered its state, raised and eventless transitions included, as a child chart does.
A <send target="#_counter"> from that step, such as the state's own <onentry>, gets error.communication. Send from a later event, as go does above.

section.heading: Answer from a timer or a promise
section.p: The invocation stays valid after the start: a service may keep it and call sendBack from a timer or a promise. It carries the invoker and the invoke:

item.text: the <param>s as an object, or the <content>;
true when a restored host starts it again ().

section.p: sendBack and done continue the invoke's trace unless their last argument is { traceparent }. A null traceparent starts a new trace.
After done, a cancel or host.close(), sendBack and done throw a TinyactorsError with TA_ERROR_STALE.
Read the send receive gets during the call, as an I/O processor's. A receive that returns a promise has its send filled first, so it may read it after an await.

section.heading: Queue sends until the service connects
section.p: A handler may return a promise of the service, while a connection opens or a process spawns. Until it settles the sends wait, and reach receive in order once it resolves.
This handler reports connecting with sendBack while it waits. Both queries reach the service once the connection opens:

example.code: status connecting db://primary says yes to first db://primary says yes to second

item.term: A cancel before the promise settles
item.text: stops the service as soon as it resolves. The sends that waited are dropped, since the invoker has left and nothing could answer them.
is a failed start: the invoker gets error.communication, once and once more for each send that waited. The rejection stays unhandled, as any handler's promise's does (Before you use it).
a promise that settles is ignored.

section.heading: Accept sends before the connection is ready
section.p: A service returned at once takes sends before it is ready, and decides itself what a send does while it connects.
This one starts connecting in its constructor, and each receive awaits that start before it asks:
await host.idle() waits for the promises your handlers return, a service handler's or a receive's. A promise a service starts on its own is yours to wait for.
Both examples open the connection in the background, so they wait on a timer before idle().

section.heading: Handle a service that fails
section.p: Each of these gives the invoker error.communication, and so does each later send until the invoker leaves the state:

item.text: no handler for the type, or none for a restored invocation;
a handler that throws or whose promise rejects;
a receive that throws or whose promise rejects: the service crashed, and is dropped without stop.

section.p: The invoker gets none when it cancelled the invocation in the same step that started it.
A handler's error is reported at the end of that event-loop turn, to onHandlerError(error, invocation) or out of idle().
A type with no handler throws nothing, since the chart chose it. An untrusted chart on quickjs cannot end your process by naming a type you do not serve.
Here the handler throws: idle() rejects with its error, then the chart handles error.communication.

example.code: idle() rejected: no SMTP server the mail service failed

section.heading: Close a host with services running
section.p: host.close() drops the running services and calls no stop. The host keeps them on its own object, so a dropped host whose services refer back to it is still collected.

section.heading: Run 200,000 services in one host
section.p: tools/services.mjs runs actors that each invoke a counter service, and sends pings and pongs to actors drawn at random. Then a third finish with done data, a third are cancelled, and the rest keep theirs.
It checks that every pong is counted once and every done datum is right. Every cancelled service must be stopped exactly once, no other stopped, and the ended services collected.

table.caption: 200,000 actors, each with a counter service, making 1,000,000 round trips (actor, service, actor); then a third finished and a third cancelled. Every check passed, and the host held only the 66,666 services still running. One run, alone on the machine, 2026-11-20: Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz, 4 CPUs, 16 GiB, Linux; Node.js 22.23.5, Bun 1.4.1.

section.p: A round trip costs about what it costs with 10,000 actors: a run's work stays the same as invocations add up.
Each invocation takes one of the host's requests. system.maxRequests sets where the pool starts, and a segment grows it when it runs out ().
In the repository, mise run services runs the program.
